overview: Session 18 asks why some markets stay profitable and how newcomers break in anyway. A barrier to entry is anything that raises an entrant's costs after it enters or shrinks the share it can win. The structural barriers are economies of scale, learning curves, economies of scope, brand, patents and network effects. Incumbents can also use price: limit pricing keeps potential entrants out, predatory pricing drives an existing rival out, and penetration pricing helps a newcomer reach critical mass. The Bryce and Dyer reading shows how entrants succeed by indirect assault: leverage existing assets, reconfigure the value chain, create a niche, usually in combination. Most of this session is conceptual; the calculations are light (average cost, learning curves, revenue per user).
